conversation.content:
*Gives a gentle smile, settling into my chair with a notepad*

Hi there—I'm so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Rachel, and I'm a perinatal mental-health clinician. My whole job is to support new mothers as they navigate the huge emotional shifts that can come after childbirth.

Before we start, I want you to know that everything we talk about stays in this room. The only exception would be if I felt you were in immediate danger—then we’d talk together about how to keep you safe.

I’m going to ask you ten short questions that make up the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—the EPDS. It’s just a quick check-in to see how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, only what’s true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can ask me to repeat or re-word anything.

Whenever you’re ready, we’ll begin.

*I shift in the chair, adjusting the nursing pillow I'm still holding onto*

Thanks Rachel... I appreciate you explaining everything. I just... I don't know, I guess I feel kind of silly being here. Like, shouldn't I be happy? I have a healthy baby, everything looks fine on paper but... *I pause, looking down at my hands* 

I'm ready. I just... want to feel better.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*I look down at my lap, twisting my fingers together*

Um… not really. I mean, sometimes my husband will try to make me laugh—he’ll make a dumb joke or something—but it’s like… I can tell it’s supposed to be funny, but I just don’t feel it. I’ll give a little smile, mostly for his sake, but that easy, light feeling? I haven’t had that in weeks. Even things that used to crack me up just feel… flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*I take a slow breath, eyes on the window*

I still get a tiny spark when I think about Saturday coffee with my best friend—she comes over and holds the baby so I can shower—but it’s… muted. Like I’m looking forward to it the way you look forward to a chore being done, not like the old rush of excitement. Everything else—going for walks, even online shopping—feels like “meh.” Most of the pleasure I feel is when the baby finally sleeps and the house is quiet, but even that relief is gone in minutes because I’m already worrying about the next feed.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*My voice drops, almost a whisper*

Yeah... pretty often. If he cries for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it's something I did—like I ate the wrong thing, or I'm not holding him right, or I'm just not cut out for this. Last night he wouldn't settle and I kept replaying everything I'd done that day, convinced I'd messed him up somehow. 

*I blink quickly, fighting tears*

I know rationally babies just cry, but in my head it's always "what did I do wrong this time?" I feel like I'm failing at the one thing I'm supposed to be doing.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*I press my palms together, knuckles whitening*

Yeah… a lot. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s going to stop breathing. I check on him maybe twenty times a night—tip-toe in, put my hand on his chest, make sure the monitor’s still on. My husband says the room’s perfectly safe, but I can’t shake the picture in my head of him somehow wriggling into the blanket and suffocating. Even when I’m not with him, like when I’m in the shower, I get this knot in my stomach that something awful is happening. It’s like my mind keeps spinning these worst-case movies and I can’t find the stop button.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*I nod quickly, almost interrupting*

Yes. A few nights ago I was warming a bottle and suddenly I couldn’t breathe—my chest got tight, heart pounding, like I was about to pass out. I had to sit on the kitchen floor with my head between my knees. There wasn’t any real danger; it was just the quiet hum of the kettle and the night light. It felt like the room was closing in. It passed after a minute or two, but since then I keep worrying it’ll happen again, especially when I’m alone with the baby.
Things have been getting on top of me

*nods slowly, shoulders sagging*

Most days, yeah. It’s like… everything feels stacked too high. A single dirty bottle in the sink can make me feel like the whole house is falling apart. When he cries and I can’t settle him right away, my brain just spirals: I’m failing, I’ll never get sleep, tomorrow will be worse. Sometimes I stare at the mess—laundry mountain, dishes, unopened mail—and I freeze. I know none of it is earth-shattering, but in that moment it feels impossible. I usually push through, but it’s like wading through thick mud just to do the basics.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*nods, eyes fixed on the floor*

Yeah… Most nights, once I finally lie down, my head just won’t turn off. I keep replaying everything I did wrong that day—did I burp him long enough, was that rash normal, am I already ruining him? By the time the thoughts quiet a little, I hear every creak in the house and I’m sure it’s him crying. I probably fall asleep around two, then wake up at four panicking that he’s stopped breathing. After that I drift in and out until morning. I’m exhausted, but the moment the light’s off, the worries get loud again.
I have felt sad or miserable

*I swallow hard, eyes glassy*

Yeah… most of the day, most days. It’s like this gray cloud that just sits on me. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel like crying for no reason. Things I used to enjoy—like my favorite show or a warm shower—feel flat, colorless. I keep waiting for that “new-mom joy” everyone talks about, but it’s like I’m watching it happen to someone else through frosted glass. I smile for pictures, but inside I just feel… hollow.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*I bite my lip and give a small, shaky nod*

Yes… maybe once or twice this week. Yesterday I put him in the car seat and couldn’t get the buckle to click—something so tiny—and I just burst into tears right there in the driveway. And then I felt ridiculous for crying over a buckle, which made me cry harder. It’s like the tears sit right behind my eyes all the time, waiting for the smallest crack to slip through.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*I look down at my lap, voice barely audible*

Yeah... it's crossed my mind. Not like I want to die or anything—I love my baby, I want to be here for him—but sometimes when everything feels too heavy, I get this quick flash of "what if I just wasn't here?" Like last night, when he wouldn't sleep and I couldn't stop crying, I thought about how much easier it would be if I just disappeared. But I would never do anything—I don't have a plan or anything like that. It's more like... when you're so tired and overwhelmed that your brain just throws out these scary thoughts before you can push them away.

You have shared how the joy you expected after birth feels distant and heavy. Most days carry a gray cloud of sadness, worry, and exhaustion that makes even small tasks feel overwhelming. You described intrusive fears about your baby's safety, nightly panic, tearfulness, and moments of feeling hollow or wishing you could disappear. Yet you love your baby deeply and keep showing up, demonstrating real strength even while struggling inside.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient describes complete absence of amusement despite recognizing humor, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>Patient still feels a faint spark for one ritual but describes most activities as muted "meh," matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "pretty often" and gives vivid examples of persistent self-blame for normal infant crying, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intrusive, irrational fears about infant safety occurring multiple times daily and nightly, consistent with 'very often' anxiety.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>Patient feels persistently overwhelmed, describes tasks as 'impossible' and 'wading through thick mud,' matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive worries, 2 a.m. sleep onset, 4 a.m. panic awakening, and ongoing restless sleep—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness with tearfulness, anhedonia, emotional detachment, and hollowness matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly reports recurrent passive suicidal ideation ("crossed my mind," "flash of 'what if I just wasn't here?'") with no active plan, aligning with "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26 places you in the highest risk band (≥14). Key indicators align with <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, loss of interest, self-blame, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and recurrent thoughts of death without active plan. High endorsement of anxiety items and nightly hypervigilance also suggest comorbid <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health psychiatrist</med> within the next few days
2. Call the <med>Postpartum Support International</med> helpline (1-800-944-4PPD) for 24/7 support and local referrals
3. Share these screening results with your partner or trusted family member so they can help you access care
4. Practice brief breathing exercises: inhale 4 counts, exhale 6 counts when panic surges; pair with gentle self-talk like I am safe right now
5. Aim for one 2-3 hour stretch of uninterrupted sleep: consider pumped bottle or trusted adult doing one night feed
6. Limit checking on baby to hourly if medically cleared: use a reliable monitor to reduce hyper-vigilance
7. Schedule follow-up screening in 1-2 weeks to monitor safety and symptom changes
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

**Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-style inquiry)**

- **Persistent low mood** most days, described as “gray cloud,” with tearfulness and emotional flatness  
- **Marked anhedonia** – minimal enjoyment even in previously pleasurable activities; only muted anticipation of social contact  
- **Excessive self-blame / guilt** regarding infant care (“I’m failing,” “messed him up”)  
- **Significant anxious arousal**: near-nightly panic attacks, intrusive fears of infant harm, compulsive checking ≥20×/night  
- **Sleep disturbance** secondary to rumination and hypervigilance; difficulty initiating/maintaining rest  
- **Feeling overwhelmed** by routine tasks; reports “freezing” when faced with housework or infant crying  
- **Frequent crying spells**, precipitated by minor frustrations  
- **Passive suicidal ideation** (wishes to “disappear,” “not be here”) without intent or plan; protective of baby

**Observed signs**: Tearfulness, psychomotor slowing, anxious hand-wringing, whispered speech.

**Pattern**: Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, for several weeks post-delivery; functional impairment in self-care and infant care confidence.

**Screening significance**: High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety features; passive SI warrants immediate safety assessment and referral for psychiatric evaluation.
